notes: Hoabinhian, a stone-tool industry (technocomplex) of mainland South-East Asia, treated as a culture; the page says it is 'dated to c. 10,000-2000 BCE' (lead) with 'artifacts from a Yunnan rock shelter ... dating from 41,500 BCE' as the earliest find and gives no end narrative; the dossier starts at -6000 and ends at the page's 2000 BCE (confidence 2). The Spirit Cave levels 'between 12,000 and 8000 BP' produced cord-marked ceramics. Extent: 'more than 120 Hoabinhian sites in Vietnam' (research intensity, not a centre), sites in Thailand (Spirit Cave, Sai Yok in Kanchanaburi), Laos (Pha Faen), Malaysia (Gua Cha in Kelantan), Cambodia, Myanmar and Sumatra, and 'the only Hoabinhian site discovered in China' (Xiaodong rockshelter, Yunnan); 'isolated inventories of stone artifacts displaying Hoabinhian elements' in southern China, Taiwan, Nepal and Australia are not sites of the industry. The shape is the five mainland countries and the Malay Peninsula, a very coarse placement of an industry known from scattered rock shelters (confidence 1 for the extent; Sumatra and the Yunnan site are not drawn). Relations: the Bacsonian is 'a variation of the Hoabinhian industry' dated 8000-4000 BCE on the Hoabinhian page; the Da But culture ('(5000-1000 BCE)', carbon-dated 'to 5000 BC', Vinh Loc district) is the 'earliest culture in the region to the post-date the Hoabinhian' (no dossier, location only a district, Thanh Hoa not on the page); Neolithic emergence 'is associated with population movements between southern China and Southeast Asia'. The page does not say when or how the Hoabinhian ended. Austroasiatic-speaking groups carry the most 'Hoabinhian-related ancestry' (a genetic remark, not drawn). No area figure.
